---
title: "Why empirical calibration is needed"
subtitle: "The nominal null is the wrong null"
---

## Two kinds of error, one standard error

Every effect estimate from an observational study is wrong by some amount. Split
that error in two.

**Random error** comes from having a finite sample. It shrinks as $1/\sqrt{n}$,
it is what the standard error measures, and it is what the entire apparatus of
confidence intervals and p-values is built to handle.

**Systematic error** comes from the study not being the experiment you wish you
had run: unmeasured confounding, selection into the cohort, misclassification of
exposure or outcome, informative censoring, and the accumulated effect of
analytic choices. It does **not** shrink with sample size. Nothing in the
standard error knows about it.

Traditional inference assumes the second category is empty. For a log relative
risk $\beta$ estimated as $\hat\beta$ with standard error $\hat\sigma$, it takes

$$
\hat\beta \sim N\!\left(\beta,\ \hat\sigma^2\right)
$$

and reports $p = 2\,\Phi\!\left(-\lvert\hat\beta\rvert/\hat\sigma\right)$ against
$\beta = 0$. If systematic error is present the location and the spread of that
sampling distribution are both wrong, so the p-value is computed against a null
the data never had a chance of following.

The consequence is not subtle. As $n$ grows, random error vanishes, systematic
error does not, and the p-value converges to zero regardless of whether there is
a real effect. **Large observational studies are reliably significant and
unreliably correct.**

## Negative controls make the error visible

A **negative control** is an exposure–outcome pair for which the true effect is
known — or as close to known as the domain allows — to be null [@lipsitch2010].
Ibuprofen does not cause ingrown toenails. If you run your study design,
unchanged, on a few dozen such pairs, then any signal that comes back is error
by construction, because the truth is zero.

That is the whole idea. You cannot see the bias in your estimate of interest,
because you do not know its true value. You *can* see the bias in estimates
whose true value you do know, and if the design's problems are not specific to
one outcome, what you see there transfers.

::: {.callout-note}
## The exchangeability assumption

Calibration assumes the systematic error affecting your hypothesis of interest
is **exchangeable** with the systematic error affecting the controls — drawn
from the same distribution. This is the assumption on which everything rests,
and it is an assumption, not a theorem. It is most credible when the controls
are numerous, chosen to resemble the outcome of interest in how they are
recorded and who gets them, and run through exactly the same pipeline. It fails
when the hypothesis of interest has a bias mechanism the controls do not share.
:::

## What the controls actually show

Running the design on negative controls and plotting the estimates against their
standard errors is diagnostic on its own. Under the theoretical null, 95% of the
controls should fall inside the region where $\lvert\hat\beta\rvert < 1.96\,\hat\sigma$.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Negative controls (blue dots) from a self-controlled case series study, plotted as estimate against standard error. The grey dashed boundary encloses the region where the traditional test calls a result significant at p < 0.05; every control inside it is a false positive, because the truth for all of them is null."
import empiricalcalibration as ec

sccs = ec.datasets.sccs()
negatives = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 0]

fig = ec.plotCalibrationEffect(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr)
```

```{python}
import numpy as np

p = ec.computeTraditionalP(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr)
print(f"negative controls:            {len(p)}")
print(f"significant at nominal 0.05:  {np.mean(p < 0.05):.0%}")
```

Every one of those is a false positive: the truth for all of them is null. A
test operating at a nominal 5% type I error rate is producing them at many times
that rate. @schuemie2014 found the same thing across a range of designs and
databases in the OMOP experiments — in several, the majority of negative
controls reached nominal significance.

This is what a mis-specified null looks like, and the fix is the one Efron
proposed for large-scale testing generally [@efron2004]: stop using the
theoretical null and estimate the null the data are actually drawn from.

## Two things calibration is not

**It is not a bias correction.** Calibration does not recover the unbiased
estimate; it does not tell you what the answer would have been in a randomized
trial. It widens and shifts your inference to reflect error you have
demonstrated is present. A calibrated interval is an honest interval, not a
corrected one.

**It is not a licence to ignore study design.** The right response to an
empirical null with a mean of 0.79 is to fix the design, not to calibrate
against it and carry on. Calibration is what you do about the residual bias you
could not eliminate — and the fitted null doubles as a scorecard telling you how
much of that there is (see [EASE](ease.qmd)).
